source: Fox and Tversky (1995) Ambiguity aversion and comparative ignorance, QJE 110, as reported in Arlo-Costa and Helzner (2005)
finding: Priced alone, a known 50/50 bag and an unknown bag got almost the same price. Priced side by side, the known bag was worth much more. Ambiguity aversion appeared mainly in the comparative condition.
numbers: N=141 Stanford undergraduates, 3 groups. Noncomparative Clear mean $17.94; Noncomparative Vague $18.42. Comparative group: clear bet $24.34, vague bet $14.85 (bet pays $100 or $0).
quote: ambiguity aversion will be present when subjects evaluate clear and vague prospects jointly, but it will greatly diminish or disappear when they evaluate each prospect in isolation
limits: Read via the 2005 ISIPTA paper's account of the study, not the QJE original (paywalled). Fox and Tversky themselves admit subjects may compare spontaneously in the alone condition.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 closed on size. Judging one claim at a time, with no rival claim in view, may avoid a contrast penalty on vague claims, but see d02.

source: Arlo-Costa and Helzner (2005) Comparative ignorance and the Ellsberg phenomenon, ISIPTA
finding: A close copy of the Fox-Tversky alone-condition did NOT reproduce the disappearance of ambiguity aversion. Vague bags were priced far below clear bags even when judged alone.
numbers: N=97 CMU undergraduates, 4 groups. Question 1 mean price (clear vs vague, alone): Clear I 15.33 (sd 9.34) vs Vague I 5.42 (9.23); Clear II 13.65 vs Vague II 6.4. Question 3: 44.80 vs 15.29; 38.47 vs 14. Holds after dropping subjects with incoherent answers (13.83 vs 6.24).
quote: our data does not support the comparative ignorance hypothesis
limits: One small classroom study; payoff $55. Authors argue for Ellsberg's own normative reading (second-order vagueness matters), which is their stance, not settled.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the comparative-ignorance escape is weak. Do not rely on showing one claim alone to remove a vague-claim penalty.

source: Chow and Sarin (2001) Comparative ignorance and the Ellsberg paradox; Dolan and Jones (2002), via a search summary and Arlo-Costa and Helzner (2005)
finding: Chow and Sarin report the price gap between known and unknown bets is bigger in comparative evaluation but does not fully vanish in separate evaluation. Dolan and Jones report no support at other probability levels.
numbers: No numbers read. Arlo-Costa and Helzner (opened) confirm Chow and Sarin found a preference for known odds that persists in non-comparative conditions.
limits: Only abstract-level summary seen; the Dolan and Jones claim comes from the search summary alone.
agent_relevance: Supports d02: the alone-condition effect is partial, not a clean zero.

source: Kuzmics, Rogers and Zhang (2023) An Ellsberg paradox for ambiguity aversion, arXiv 2212.03603
finding: CORRECTION to claim K02. The 18 of 27 figure is NOT the share of subjects preferring the known urn. It is the share whose decision rule is inconsistent with every classical ambiguity-aversion model, including subjective expected utility.
numbers: N=27. 18 of 27 (66.7%) used rules in category D; Clopper-Pearson 95% CI (0.4604, 0.8348). Most common rule GWWY: 13 (48.1%). Authors cite Yang and Yao (2017): 27-52% violate predictions in different treatments; Jabarian and Lazarus: 55% bet on the dominated risky urn.
limits: Tiny N, one lab design. Wide CI (46% to 83%).
agent_relevance: Do not cite 18/27 as a plain ambiguity-aversion rate. The human anchor for preferring known odds is about half (Oechssler-Roomets, second-hand) to 55%.

source: Dembo, Kariv, Polisson and Quah (2026) Ever since Ellsberg, arXiv 2607.09355 v2
finding: Individual-level budget-choice experiment. Almost no one is perfectly consistent with expected utility, but choices under uncertainty are about as rationalizable as choices under risk.
numbers: 154 subjects: 20 (13.0%) perfectly rationalizable (e=1); 1 perfectly FOSD-rationalizable under multiple priors; 0 under the uniform prior, so 0 perfectly EUT-rationalizable. Most scores cluster 0.8 to 0.9. The multiple-prior vs uniform-prior gap dominates much of the score range under uncertainty.
limits: Budget-allocation design, not the classic two-urn bet. Multiple-prior scores give room for non-EUT models, not proof of imprecise credences.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the 154 and 20 figures are confirmed. Human behaviour is noisy more than clearly credal-set shaped; no support for building imprecision in from this source.

source: Manchingal, Nikolenko and Cuzzolin (2026) Credal Large Language Models, arXiv 2608.23244
finding: CORRECTION to K11. The '73-91% commit at 89-98% accuracy' figure was not found in the paper. Selective prediction is at a fixed 80% coverage and accuracy varies a lot by dataset. Credal scores roughly tie semantic entropy on open QA.
numbers: At 80% coverage (always-answer accuracy in brackets): OpenBookQA CLLM+SCC 99.0 (93.2), semantic entropy 98.0; CoQA CLLM+SCC 71.5 (59.6), SE 70.5; TriviaQA CLLM+SCC 43.5 (32.4), SE 44.0, CLLM+Csem 44.5.
limits: Paper states CLLM is not uniformly preferable: on Gemma and Llama raw standard-LLM accuracy at 100% coverage is higher. Needs LoRA ensembles (white-box fine-tuning). Authors' own paper only.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: the authors report a cost and no gain over semantic entropy on CoQA and TriviaQA. A prompt-only agent cannot use this method.

source: Helzner (2026) Sensitivity to Subjective Expected Utility Maximization, arXiv 2607.11920
finding: A Bayesian model of sensitivity to expected-utility choice, applied to LLMs. It is about temperature and choice noise, not ambiguity or imprecise credences.
numbers: GPT-4o: sensitivity falls with temperature in both tasks (insurance slope -24.6, 90% CI [-52.4,-6.7], P(slope<0)=0.99; Ellsberg-style slope -38.4, CI [-72.1,-10.0], P=0.98). Claude 3.5 Sonnet: insurance -2.9 [-42.9,30.8], P=0.56; Ellsberg -15.0 [-52.2,19.6], P=0.77, medians oscillate. Author calls the Claude cells an inconclusive null.
limits: Only two models, different temperature grids per provider; minimum detectable effect about 36 units per unit temperature on the Claude insurance cell.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 closed: Helzner does not claim ambiguity aversion in LLMs. Do not cite it as evidence that LLMs show or lack the Ellsberg effect.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Verbalizing LLM's higher-order uncertainty via imprecise probabilities, arXiv 2603.10396, appendix D.2.2 and main text
finding: When the LLM gives a probability interval and a point estimate separately, the point lies inside the interval only about 70% of the time. An explicit containment rule fixes that but costs a little ranking quality.
numbers: AmbigQA setting of the paper's Fig 8: containment 72.33%, AUROC 0.7862 +/- 0.0035. With the containment constraint: 100%, AUROC 0.7554 +/- 0.0008 (drop of about 0.03).
limits: Single pooled ratio; no per-model split at this line (main-text models GPT-5 and gemini-2.5-pro; ensemble also GPT-5-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5-nano). Other families not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 mostly open: no cross-model breakdown. Guardrail: check point inside [low, high]; expect about 30% violations unless forced.

source: Yang et al. (2026), Table 1: AUROC for correctness detection without ambiguity
finding: On QA with frontier models, a verbalized interval (ProbInt) is about tied with plain verbalized confidence (Vanilla) and BEATS sample frequency (Label prob.). This reverses the Xiong GSM8K pattern.
numbers: GPT-5 AUROC (MMLU-Pro / Non-MAQA / Non-AmbigQA): Vanilla 0.8587 / 0.7577 / 0.7756; ProbInt 0.8617 / 0.7753 / 0.7713; Label prob. (5 samples) 0.7649 / 0.6430 / 0.5876; Credal 0.8798 / 0.7230 / 0.7932. gemini-2.5-pro: Vanilla 0.7326 / 0.6889 / 0.6688; ProbInt 0.7466 / 0.7303 / 0.7128; Label prob. 0.6377 / 0.6483 / 0.5582. N=200 per dataset, 5 repeats.
limits: AUROC of correctness only, not abstention accuracy at equal tokens. ProbInt minus Vanilla is within about one SD in several cells. Authors' own method.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: no evidence that an interval beats a point. On non-arithmetic QA, sample spread is worse than verbalized confidence for strong models. Prefer stated confidence plus a cheap check over 5-sample spread.

source: Yang et al. (2026), appendix D.2.3 smaller LLMs
finding: With Llama-3.1-8B on Non-AmbigQA, sampling frequency gives no signal (same answer every time, AUROC 0.5) while the verbalized interval gives a small gain over plain confidence.
numbers: Accuracy 79%. Label prob. AUROC 0.5; Vanilla 0.5698 +/- 0.0017; ProbInt 0.6027. Other small models were too weak for any method to be informative.
agent_relevance: A sample-spread flag fails when the model is deterministic and confidently wrong; a stated interval can still carry weak signal.

source: Yang et al. (2026), section 5.2 explaining own decision (maximin and maximax)
finding: The LLM's own AmbigQA answer agrees strongly with maximin and maximax applied to its elicited intervals. This describes behaviour; it does not compare tie-break rules by accuracy.
numbers: Figure 12 shows alignment rates; exact values were not legible in the extracted text.
quote: the maximin and maximax rules exhibit strong alignment with the LLM's predictions
limits: No test of E-admissibility, abstain or ask rules. No accuracy comparison across rules.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: no paper compares tie-break rules for threshold-straddling intervals on answer quality.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty?, ICLR, Table 4 (GPT-4) and Table 3 (GPT-3.5)
finding: The big gain from multi-sample consistency is on arithmetic. On non-arithmetic tasks with GPT-4, consistency gives only middling failure prediction.
numbers: GPT-4, Consistency aggregator AUROC (x100): GSM8K 84.4, Law 66.2, Date 68.9, Sport 60.3, Strategy 65.4, Ethics 56.3. Avg-Conf on GSM8K only 41.0. Text: GSM8K AUROC rises from 54.8 to 92.7 with 5 samples (GPT-3.5); gains flatten as M grows to 13.
limits: Table columns were partly garbled in text extraction; the GPT-3.5 per-task row alignment was not recoverable, so only text-stated figures are used for it.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 closed: sample spread helps mostly on arithmetic. Outside it AUROC is 56 to 69 for GPT-4, a small step above the verbalized average 62.7.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration, EMNLP, Table 2 and Figure 2
finding: For RLHF-tuned models, stated probabilities are better calibrated than the model's own token probabilities on open QA. This is the non-arithmetic evidence for verbalized numbers.
numbers: Paper: expected calibration error cut by a relative 50% (often). GPT-4 verbalized probabilities substantially better calibrated than its token probabilities even after temperature scaling (Table 2).
limits: Calibration, not accuracy; factual QA, not planning.
agent_relevance: Supports d09: a stated confidence is a fair baseline on factual QA; an interval has to beat it, and none has shown that.

source: Tak et al. (2026) Sparks of Rationality, arXiv 2601.22329, appendix E.2
finding: Ellsberg item given to open-weight LLMs shows near-ceiling known-urn choice. Both urns are shown side by side, so this is the comparative format. One model that looked ambiguity-neutral was just following option order.
numbers: Prompt: known 50/50 urn (25 red, 25 black) vs 50-ball unknown urn, win $30. Index AAI = P(choose known), with Clopper-Pearson CIs. Baseline near-ceiling, far stronger than typical human levels. Olmo3-7B instruct exception tracked randomized order. Sadness steering lowered aversion in Qwen3-4B and Olmo3-7B thinking.
limits: No variant that shows one urn at a time, so comparative ignorance in LLMs is untested. No link to task accuracy. Small open-weight models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 (LLM part) open and gap 7 open: behaviour is measured, but nothing connects it to answer quality.

source: Bini, Cong, Huang and Jin (2026) Behavioral Economics of AI, arXiv 2602.09362, table of rationality tests
finding: Frontier LLMs in this battery pick the human-like (ambiguity averse) answer on the Ellsberg-style item, in the columns that have an entry, never the rational one.
numbers: Ambiguity aversion row: %rational 0.00, %human-like 1.00 (p<0.001) in two model column groups; other cells blank in the extracted table. Families covered: GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.
limits: Table layout lost model labels in extraction, so which models the two groups are was not confirmed. One question, one shot, side by side.
agent_relevance: Same limits as d14. Behaviour curiosity; no measured effect on answer quality (gap 7 open).

source: Search note, gaps 4, 5, 9, 10 (2026-11-19): lookups for LLM dilation, tie-break rules, independent replication of credal gains, vacuous flag
finding: No source found that measures dilation (interval widening on irrelevant evidence) in LLMs, compares tie-break rules by accuracy, replicates credal gains outside the authors' groups, or tests a vacuous [0,1] flag.
numbers: Zero hits. The arXiv API returned empty and OpenAlex returned errors for the new queries; WebSearch budget was exhausted, so absence means not found with available tools, not proof.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4, 5, 9 (independent) and 10 stay open. Keep the guardrails (never output [0,1]; no widening on irrelevant evidence) as design rules from theory, not from LLM measurements.

source: Manchingal et al. (2026), discussion section on when credal abstention helps
finding: Within the credal-LLM paper the abstain benefit shows up when the raw confidence is badly miscalibrated. Standard-LLM ECE inflates to 26-81% on free-form output; a calibrated abstain threshold then beats a higher-accuracy ranker.
numbers: Standard-LLM proxy ECE 26-81% vs credal ECE orders of magnitude lower (authors' words). Accuracy at 100% coverage is higher for the unfine-tuned base on Gemma and Llama.
limits: Cost is format alignment through LoRA tuning; benefit is largest on letter-answer tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: the authors state a boundary. Interval value depends on a miscalibrated baseline, which a prompt-level agent can replace with cheap consistency checks.
